questions.problem:
$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t)=3x(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t)=7y(t)\end{aligned}
$$

Which of the following could represent the phase portrait of the decoupled system above?
questions.worked_solution:
Writing our system in matrix form, we have

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}3 & 0 \\ 0 & 7\end{aligned}]x(t)
$$

where $x(t)=[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}].$

Since our system is decoupled, its eigenvectors are the following:

- Eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1}=3$ with the corresponding eigenvector $[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}].$

- Eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{2}=7$ with the corresponding eigenvector $[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$

The general solution of the system is

$$
x(t)={c}_{1}{e}^{3t}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]+{c}_{2}{e}^{7t}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Now, notice that:

- The straight-line solutions of the form
${c}_{1}{e}^{3t}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]$
lie on the $x$-axis. Since ${e}^{3t}\to \infty $ as $t\to \infty ,$ these solutions approach infinity as $t\to \infty .$

- The straight-line solutions of the form
${c}_{2}{e}^{7t}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]$
lie on the $y$-axis. Since ${e}^{7t}\to \infty $ as $t\to \infty ,$ these solutions approach infinity as $t\to \infty .$

Among the given options, the only phase portrait satisfying these conditions is the following:

Which of the following could represent the phase portrait of the decoupled system above?

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14121715/assets/040ac76a28687db1c99d3379242b726a85aa4baf269a7c6d35d9662af1d3bd78.png)

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14121715/assets/0c10626785034f566b65778fad63032e3a9ad8cc2c884bc3da3e88fdff3db50b.svg)
where ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14121715/assets/18d25c282ee921144387d9c30e19a461746271a44cab929ab8075190b0f5c16e.svg)

Since our system is decoupled, its eigenvectors are the following:

- Eigenvalue $\lambda_1=4$ with the corresponding eigenvector ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14121715/assets/e99452a0ae70ad466de402da561590e4fc3b0de089fa0f74818a1986cadfbd42.svg)

- Eigenvalue $\lambda_2=-6$ with the corresponding eigenvector ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14121715/assets/50b227b577144e091543a383e38d0d74a02193b8372fec1eddcfa75d06d3878b.svg)

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14121715/assets/0ee79c93c2e488563f7515fb0ec6b30d5cb2b41795d23f0b9d4699338edcc92c.svg)

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14121715/assets/517dcfcf2467960dd5d35d9676c86c4bf0f66e0c4f13ccd99e862816efed675e.svg)

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Identifying the Phase Portrait of a System

canonical_examples.name:
Example: 
                    Identifying the System Given a Phase Portrait
canonical_examples.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14121715/assets/25d4f77a3f596202229581e06d88a9e3bdd84dc6b8b7e14b6f46b3b3d2f125d2.png)

Consider the phase portrait for a decoupled system above.
Which of the following systems could correspond to the given portrait?

I. ${\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t)=-5x(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t)=6y(t)\end{aligned}$

II. ${\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t)=5x(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t)=6y(t)\end{aligned}$

III. ${\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t)=5x(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t)=-6y(t)\end{aligned}$

IV. ${\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t)=-5x(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t)=-6y(t)\end{aligned}$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Writing a decoupled system in matrix form, we have
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14121715/assets/50b547a3223fe85dde50b06d78ee35bfff49d95c43a4ebadcc2d1007ac041eb1.svg)
where ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14121715/assets/ee1bb1b6a9869493ae3bcfaa42d63d07b6054aaa19f25c9fa8a2665e9642e0be.svg)

Since our system is decoupled, its eigenvectors are parallel to the axes. These correspond to so-called straight-line solutions of the form
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14121715/assets/853be349a48d204b073b1ad3aaa709df082bd7fa5163aec09d5364836918a9e6.svg)

Now, notice that:

- The tangents along the $x$-axis are pointing toward the origin, meaning that the solutions of the form 
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14121715/assets/5903874b33d77f242d725ad16fffef59ee24e1bde4210128ed590031ddc43e99.svg)
must approach the origin as $t \to \infty.$ So, we must have $\lambda_1 < 0.$

- The tangents along the $y$-axis are also pointing toward the origin, meaning that the solutions of the form 
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14121715/assets/856d5a86b76c30e0601803216465f29a1e3bd7fb993a58ee6ba85ba7c0627fd9.svg)
must also approach the origin as $t \to \infty.$ So, we must have $\lambda_2 < 0.$

Among the options, the only system that satisfies $\lambda_1 < 0$ and $\lambda_2 < 0$ is the following:

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t)=-5x(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t)=-6y(t)\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Identifying the System Given a Phase Portrait

canonical_examples.name:
Example: 
                    Identifying the Phase Portrait Given a System: Advanced Cases
canonical_examples.problem:
$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t)=-x(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t)=-4y(t)\end{aligned}
$$

Which of the following could represent the phase portrait of the decoupled system above?

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14121715/assets/470210fb9509e87c3e51a990bac7483e5862d2f37afdce9823279838e8391592.png)
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Writing our system in matrix form, we have
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14121715/assets/cc4019b4978cb96b931632ee2b6bf318b5eda46f4d9a73d252e76c7572285517.svg)
where ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14121715/assets/458d9c56e8c1857546e7e112a9ad084fe7832781d448340ccfc141438a6eee78.svg)

Since our system is decoupled, its eigenvectors are the following:

- Eigenvalue $\lambda_1=-1$ with the corresponding eigenvector ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14121715/assets/d504ae47c4cfcd428a362d590d23713844d9ead5df792086a3bab07d41573bd8.svg)

- Eigenvalue $\lambda_2=-4$ with the corresponding eigenvector ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14121715/assets/9210f84189ff4a94c1a1dded19ff6e409c75be9d4e27f17d4d1a4d9ff44fcc0b.svg)

The general solution of the system is
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14121715/assets/38e227b8bac9c4cb2ae93e2b29e1ca70576383a176dcf193350a9b464a4dd88f.svg)

Now, notice that:

- The straight-line solutions of the form
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14121715/assets/7ef739bcc9a338d9535ab130a3bbe1cd46204bf7d8dbd55a49244abe9764a04a.svg)
lie on the $x$-axis. Since $e^{-t} \to 0$ as $t \to \infty,$ these solutions approach the origin as $t \to \infty.$

- The straight-line solutions of the form
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14121715/assets/924dcd7002fa679bf3a0021099928c45fba82a5bf54ba157a21d846eb1587640.svg)
lie on the $y$-axis. Since $e^{-4t} \to 0$ as $t \to \infty,$ these solutions also approach the origin as $t \to \infty.$

Among the given options, there are two phase portraits satisfying these conditions:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14121715/assets/c5b1aa6ccde39c56b503e2d59a56e2ac8058b08495567f4e2cb40f6a056faedd.png)

Let's consider the solutions $x(t) = c_1e^{-t}$ and $y(t)=c_2e^{-4t}$ provided that $c_1,c_2 \neq 0.$ Then,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{{y}^{′}(t)}{{x}^{′}(t)}=\frac{({c}_{2}{e}^{-4t})^{′}}{({c}_{1}{e}^{-t})^{′}}=\frac{-4{c}_{2}{e}^{-4t}}{-{c}_{1}{e}^{-t}}=\frac{4{c}_{2}}{{c}_{1}}{e}^{-3t}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, $\dfrac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} \to 0$ as $t \to \infty,$ meaning that the tangents to the solution become more and more horizontal as the trajectories approach the origin. This corresponds to the following phase portrait:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14121715/assets/6c3af2fe68c4bcddbbfd9f13eb84e73014511374c0adc570084f9c92773d31e0.png)

canonical_examples.name:
Example: 
                    Classifying Decoupled Systems of Linear Differential Equations
canonical_examples.problem:
$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t)=2x(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t)=4y(t)\end{aligned}
$$

Interpret the stability of the $x$-axis, the $y$-axis, and the equilibrium point (the origin) for the given decoupled system of linear differential equations.
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Writing our system in matrix form, we have
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14121715/assets/73afc7cad8d4018e66ce31d26275c6d3238e0b50bfc85c65c84abb3d1d9c3c3c.svg)
where ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14121715/assets/375392fe3e7223efb30963c4f51b76a08f868bdde210574bb8fb0f2e53f925be.svg)

Recall that a homogeneous system of linear differential equations has a single equilibrium (fixed point) at the origin.

Since our system is decoupled, its eigenvectors are the following:

- Eigenvalue $\lambda_1=2$ with the eigenvector ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14121715/assets/b8dce83f78184c194c43b2cf2b4148549a4ff0504a0f663f6a338a8cca6dec2f.svg) The corresponding straight-line solutions of the form
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14121715/assets/796f9e0b1c5698e87439547b5c84e00d492a6c7893cfd6adb793bd0639147d25.svg)
lie on the $x$-axis and move away from the origin as $t \to \infty.$ So, the $x$-axis is the $\bbox[4pt, border: solid 1pt gainsboro]{\text{unstable}}$ line.

- Eigenvalue $\lambda_2=4$ with the eigenvector ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14121715/assets/f9da7bff2e0d90f112ce26291e3c1074e766e141bdae4198870d49136ed6706a.svg) The corresponding straight-line solutions of the form
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14121715/assets/9d8a16728992f0ce055be81c84ae0e905417e2ed74c4e659b277ab7f4226e90a.svg)
lie on the $y$-axis and also move away from the origin as $t \to \infty.$ So, the $y$-axis is the $\bbox[4pt, border: solid 1pt gainsboro]{\text{unstable}}$ line.

Therefore, the equilibrium point (origin) is $\bbox[4pt, border: solid 1pt gainsboro]{\text{an unstable node (source)}}.$ 

**Note:** The phase portrait of the system looks as follows:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14121715/assets/2b79201d15fe5d2a9896cdee09c0474b97bb933d75fcf478c6fdb37cb4d16742.png)

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Classifying Decoupled Systems of Linear Differential Equations

tutorials.name: Introduction
tutorials.problem:
Consider a *decoupled* linear system of ODEs
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14121715/assets/3f7a114fa75100f8cd3ccf72822758e668f3a6a0824ad5f5437ebef138928fb5.svg)

In this lesson, we consider only decoupled systems with nonzero eigenvalues ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14121715/assets/77bce8fda831b5be2b2f52e043375447e794f8dad01a666d45e08716e912d707.svg) and ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14121715/assets/b8ed089264b88bdcf4018f44db6dade448063b56a6ded558fb74d7c2ca61c0de.svg) so the origin is the equilibrium point we will classify.

Recall that the eigenvalues for a diagonal matrix are its diagonal entries, ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14121715/assets/77bce8fda831b5be2b2f52e043375447e794f8dad01a666d45e08716e912d707.svg) and ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14121715/assets/afb536c2c395100d85543d9c25f58d867e0bcfbd5f826d794284b648e7cc0550.svg) 
The corresponding eigenvectors are parallel to the coordinate axes:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14121715/assets/8337ebfc4aae4b8e97438cdba58872082bdc8965932659fdf2f8ff9cf061b375.svg)

So, the general solution of the system is given by
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14121715/assets/fcb5c1cea49dfe7aa1058f64d859a8b47c363f7f6195bf68056b18f1fa6d37f2.svg)

Notice that if a solution starts on one of the coordinate axes, it remains on that axis. These are called **straight-line solutions**:

- On the ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14121715/assets/fcc5df999e3b49fae1685ee0ab5bd03709804e1dd49f2ee722c4269eb0f5506d.svg)-axis (![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14121715/assets/8da7ef7a61d4c5af4d28575fcd263714cf3bda8e7d94985bd4bea5c03eb2d53f.svg)): 
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14121715/assets/aa9cd3c49609ee6d09a61c9c31438e4297620feedfda1073fbc55c08e7c53d01.svg)

- On the ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14121715/assets/1d9b846cface9f9348e4081a0dd87dd254bf26663c12aa0d1a15aa24d2393261.svg)-axis (![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14121715/assets/f271ee76900762067d886b30871a9ea7538ae69318ad4514e5b39cfdce12644b.svg)):
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14121715/assets/509154a662b215d445b282396a8f43828e582d43282467a0da73843ade7ec5d8.svg)

The stability of these solutions as ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14121715/assets/919e9a7f2e074404c564846d6d8e1576e63b42ecbcc768b97d0632c645e32f22.svg) depends on the *signs* of the eigenvalues ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14121715/assets/77bce8fda831b5be2b2f52e043375447e794f8dad01a666d45e08716e912d707.svg) and ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14121715/assets/afb536c2c395100d85543d9c25f58d867e0bcfbd5f826d794284b648e7cc0550.svg) We will explore the three main stability cases in the upcoming examples.

tutorials.name: One Positive and One Negative Eigenvalue
tutorials.problem:
Suppose we have a decoupled system

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t)={\lambda }_{1}x(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t)={\lambda }_{2}y(t)\end{aligned}
$$

where $\lambda_1>0$ and $\lambda_2<0$ (the opposite case, where $\lambda_1<0$ and $\lambda_2>0,$ is similar). 

Let's now determine the behavior along the axes.

- The straight-line solutions on the $x$-axis have the form ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14121715/assets/4dc3aaf0f7dfd85070df84c13abe2cf02d85a704167569b3d3a76f2b58178c5b.svg) Since $\lambda_1>0,$ we have that $e^{\lambda_1 t} \to \infty$ as $t \to \infty.$ Thus, the trajectories on the $x$-axis move *away* from the origin. This is called an **unstable axis**.

- The straight-line solutions on the $y$-axis have the form ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14121715/assets/76f6b9bbcdff2c87295fb0cd14dbdbbaa5e6c75eeb49c1cc158a4e8bd3da059d.svg) Since $\lambda_2<0,$ we have that $e^{\lambda_2 t} \to 0$ as $t \to \infty.$ Thus, the trajectories on the $y$-axis move *toward* the origin. This is called a **stable axis**.

Because one axis is stable and the other is unstable, the origin (equilibrium point) is called a **saddle point**.

tutorials.title: One Positive and One Negative Eigenvalue
tutorials.content:
Suppose we have a decoupled system

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t)={\lambda }_{1}x(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t)={\lambda }_{2}y(t)\end{aligned}
$$

where $\lambda_1>0$ and $\lambda_2<0$ (the opposite case, where $\lambda_1<0$ and $\lambda_2>0,$ is similar). 

Let's now determine the behavior along the axes.

- The straight-line solutions on the $x$-axis have the form ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14121715/assets/4dc3aaf0f7dfd85070df84c13abe2cf02d85a704167569b3d3a76f2b58178c5b.svg) Since $\lambda_1>0,$ we have that $e^{\lambda_1 t} \to \infty$ as $t \to \infty.$ Thus, the trajectories on the $x$-axis move *away* from the origin. This is called an **unstable axis**.

- The straight-line solutions on the $y$-axis have the form ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14121715/assets/76f6b9bbcdff2c87295fb0cd14dbdbbaa5e6c75eeb49c1cc158a4e8bd3da059d.svg) Since $\lambda_2<0,$ we have that $e^{\lambda_2 t} \to 0$ as $t \to \infty.$ Thus, the trajectories on the $y$-axis move *toward* the origin. This is called a **stable axis**.

Because one axis is stable and the other is unstable, the origin (equilibrium point) is called a **saddle point**.

In the phase portrait, we draw

- arrows on the $x$-axis pointing *outward* (away from the origin), while

- arrows on the $y$-axis pointing *inward* (toward the origin).

A typical trajectory bends from the stable direction and then peels away along the unstable direction.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14121715/assets/f2538a59050e604d85fd9726e688cfbd2a5c9bdff4d15dd5ed465ed04f7290b4.png)

tutorials.name: Dominant Eigenvalue
tutorials.problem:
For a decoupled system
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14121715/assets/df904ec5214399987c94f99323d3c3c4c06d9e19242c0d580574488011475acc.svg)
we know the *signs* of ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14121715/assets/77bce8fda831b5be2b2f52e043375447e794f8dad01a666d45e08716e912d707.svg) and ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14121715/assets/c0413ea28006ddd6542ba7f9ebf2714b6091aca8fa79396d545b48db347c3a80.svg) tell us the type of the equilibrium (sink/source/saddle). But how can we determine the shape of trajectories in cases when the origin is a source (![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14121715/assets/bb6302eab08feb0614c62d4ea8012676675715a469dd30a7321ec228ff7ef4e9.svg)) or a sink (![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14121715/assets/be8860e40a1c229262d3bf3375732f4b4583cad7aaf63f3a17e871bbd5a51abb.svg))?

To do this, we can compare the rates of change of ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14121715/assets/f7dbfa03976240534a1b57f2cc59c474401a0d9524bc5f627736da01a0d775c1.svg) and ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14121715/assets/cc436bde605f3822acb66d36528ba42a812a50fdbea361b31f0dbd0cba61d810.svg) by looking at the slope of the tangent line to the trajectory, ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14121715/assets/c7244a31f756199a29c0e7e755eccdf9274346e643e0856566469b35a207e53a.svg) Assuming ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14121715/assets/371aec72d3e326e3e52fbd1a1cfc06be06b33e3054e60b8c286a9fcbac39141e.svg) we have:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14121715/assets/be21baf0c518d85b105b0f569382fbc47075c268847437046b042db36a9b4b8a.svg)

As we can see, the long-term behavior of the slope as ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14121715/assets/919e9a7f2e074404c564846d6d8e1576e63b42ecbcc768b97d0632c645e32f22.svg) depends on the sign of the exponent, ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14121715/assets/7cde6653feb562f0d136150bffa6f2925af0c7dbcb9ede5c7f1b3e0f10f3796d.svg)

This comparison is governed by which eigenvalue is larger. We call the larger eigenvalue (the one that is more positive, or less negative) the **dominant eigenvalue**.

In the next slides, we will analyze the source and sink cases separately.

tutorials.name: Classification of Equilibria
tutorials.problem:
Finally, let’s summarize what we’ve learned so far.

Again, we are considering a decoupled linear system
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14121715/assets/e1efdd0b8c037c01450042384ce3bac663d0b549fa9557d0db09b692754cab0f.svg)

Recall that a homogeneous linear system has a single equilibrium point at the origin $(0,0).$ 
To classify this equilibrium, we look at the signs of $\lambda_1$ and $\lambda_2.$

First of all, the coordinate axes are straight-line solutions:

- On the $x$-axis, we have $y(t)= 0$ and $x(t)=c_1e^{\lambda_1 t}$.

- If $\lambda_1<0,$ the $x$-axis is a *stable* line.

- If $\lambda_1>0,$ the $x$-axis is an *unstable* line.

- On the $y$-axis, we have $x(t)=0$ and $y(t)=c_2e^{\lambda_2 t}.$

- If $\lambda_2<0,$ the $y$-axis is a *stable* line.

- If $\lambda_2>0,$ the $y$-axis is an *unstable* line.

As for the classification of the equilibrium at the origin, we get the following:

- *Unstable node (source)* if $\lambda_1>0$ and $\lambda_2>0.$

- *Stable node (sink)* if $\lambda_1<0$ and $\lambda_2<0.$ In fact, it's asymptotically stable, as the trajectories converge to the origin.

- *Saddle point* if $\lambda_1\lambda_2<0$ (one positive, one negative).

Let's see some examples.

tutorials.title: Classification of Equilibria
tutorials.content:
Finally, let’s summarize what we’ve learned so far.

Again, we are considering a decoupled linear system
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14121715/assets/e1efdd0b8c037c01450042384ce3bac663d0b549fa9557d0db09b692754cab0f.svg)

Recall that a homogeneous linear system has a single equilibrium point at the origin $(0,0).$ 
To classify this equilibrium, we look at the signs of $\lambda_1$ and $\lambda_2.$

First of all, the coordinate axes are straight-line solutions:

- On the $x$-axis, we have $y(t)= 0$ and $x(t)=c_1e^{\lambda_1 t}$.

- If $\lambda_1<0,$ the $x$-axis is a *stable* line.

- If $\lambda_1>0,$ the $x$-axis is an *unstable* line.

- On the $y$-axis, we have $x(t)=0$ and $y(t)=c_2e^{\lambda_2 t}.$

- If $\lambda_2<0,$ the $y$-axis is a *stable* line.

- If $\lambda_2>0,$ the $y$-axis is an *unstable* line.

As for the classification of the equilibrium at the origin, we get the following:

- *Unstable node (source)* if $\lambda_1>0$ and $\lambda_2>0.$

- *Stable node (sink)* if $\lambda_1<0$ and $\lambda_2<0.$ In fact, it's asymptotically stable, as the trajectories converge to the origin.

- *Saddle point* if $\lambda_1\lambda_2<0$ (one positive, one negative).

Let's see some examples.
